chapter: Vernon Andrade's band and Harlem life
title: Vernon Andrade's house band at the Renaissance Casino
summary: Caldwell played Thursday through Sunday with Andrade at the Renaissance, with a regular personnel and arrangements copied from Duke records.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it

blocks.x: Sure, he was. Now it says 'Regularly'
(Unintelligible) with Vernon Andrade " Andrott's -- is that the way you pronounce it?
That's right.
" From 1929 until 1933."
Right.
Where was that?

At the Renaissance -- we'd be up to the Renaissance Casino. That's where he had -- was stationed there, used to play all the big basketball games and big clubs, a lot of big, negro old clubs like the Cosmopolitans Club, big (unintelligible) clubs and Vernon was with the house band there, and in the house band --
Was that playing every night?
Well, say, from Thursday, Friday, Saturday and some double on Sunday.
Oh, so that was a good gig.
Yes, a very good gig, got paid every night too. And then we went up to Savoy too.
Well, did he keep a band more or less regular personnel?

Yes, he did. During the -- when the ballroom would, say, close down in June, July and August, we'd go and get some jobs, like on a summer job, and they went right back again in September. Lot of us sometime would go down to the Lafayette Lockvat Theater pit for the summer.
Well, who was in the band with you?
Well, they were Louie Metcalf on trumpet, George Washington Charlie Weiser on trombone, Al Morgan on bass, Zootie Simmons on drums and Clarence Wheeler on trumpet.
Clarence who?
Clarence Wheeler, on trumpet.
Oh, Wheeler, yeah.

And Andrade (unintelligible) was playing banjo, and then the reed section was myself and Gene Mikell still living, -- used to (unintelligible) and Gene's still playing. And WYNTON Thompson, one of the fellows -- one of the members of that Down magazine club, and he had a fine matter of fact, ten piece (band unintelligible). That's when the band was actually formalized. But he had a band before that. Then he started to change, and the men would be a little more on the swing side.
Well, did -- who would do the arrangements for this?
Well, Louie Metcalf and Rinkton Thompson would take them off the records, like some of Duke's melodies, take them off the records and write them out for the band.
So I mean it's like a -- it was a good gig and quite a good band but not sort of like quite the top.
